per_question.question: What DME items are specifically NOT covered by NC Medicaid under the Orthotics and Prosthetics policy, and what general criteria must be met for coverage?
per_question.agent_answer:
Under NC Medicaid Clinical Coverage Policy 5B, the Orthotics & Prosthetics policy does **not** cover certain categories of items, and coverage generally requires that the device be ordered, medically necessary, tied to the beneficiary’s condition and treatment plan, and supported by a recent face-to-face encounter. The current authoritative document is Policy 5B, with no amendments returned in the amendment check. [Orthotics & Prosthetics](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/5b-orthotics-prosthetics/download?attachment)

## Items specifically not covered

### Item-specific exclusions
Policy 5B specifically says Medicaid does **not** cover:

- **Devices for the beneficiary’s comfort or convenience**, or for the convenience of the beneficiary’s caregiver(s)
- **Backup devices** or **duplicate devices** to keep at different locations
- **Devices and supplies for residents of nursing facilities**
- **Devices or supplies covered by another agency**
- **Equipment or supplies for beneficiaries receiving hospice care** as defined in Subsection 7.3, Coordinating Care  
  [Orthotics & Prosthetics](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/5b-orthotics-prosthetics/download?attachment) § 4.2.1

### General noncoverage rules
In addition, the policy generally does **not** cover a product, procedure, or service when:

- the beneficiary does not meet Section 2.0 eligibility requirements;
- the beneficiary does not meet the coverage criteria in Section 3.0;
- the item or service duplicates another provider’s item or service; or
- it is **experimental, investigational, or part of a clinical trial**.  
  [Orthotics & Prosthetics](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/5b-orthotics-prosthetics/download?attachment) § 4.1

## General criteria that must be met for coverage

To be covered, orthotic or prosthetic devices must meet these baseline criteria:

- be **ordered by a physician, physician assistant, or nurse practitioner**;
- be **medically necessary** to maintain or improve the beneficiary’s medical, physical, or functional level;
- be **appropriate for use in a noninstitutional setting** where normal life activities take place;
- be supported by a **documented face-to-face encounter** with the ordering physician, PA, or NP related to the primary reason for the device, occurring **no more than 6 months before** initiation of the orthotic or prosthetic;
- have the beneficiary’s need **reviewed at least annually** by the ordering physician, PA, or NP.  
  [Orthotics & Prosthetics](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/5b-orthotics-prosthetics/download?attachment) § 3.2.1

### Additional medical-necessity standards
The policy also requires that orthotic and prosthetic devices be:

- a **reasonable and medically necessary** part of the beneficiary’s treatment plan;
- **consistent with the beneficiary’s diagnosis and medical condition**, especially the beneficiary’s functional limitations and symptoms; and
- **of high quality**, with replacement parts available and obtainable.  
  [Orthotics & Prosthetics](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/5b-orthotics-prosthetics/download?attachment) § 3.2.1

### How the policy defines medical necessity for orthotics vs. prosthetics
- **Orthotic devices** are medically necessary when required to **correct or prevent skeletal deformities**, **support or align movable body parts**, or **preserve or improve physical function**.
- **Prosthetic devices** are medically necessary when they **replace all or part of the function of a permanently inoperative, absent, or malfunctioning body part**, and the beneficiary requires the prosthesis for **mobility, daily care, or rehabilitation purposes**.  
  [Orthotics & Prosthetics](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/5b-orthotics-prosthetics/download?attachment) § 3.2.1

## Documentation-related criteria
As a secondary documentation point, Attachment E repeats that the requested device must fit the definition of an orthotic or prosthetic, be safe, effective, economical, medical in nature, and not intended for convenience; it also says it must not be experimental or investigational. [Orthotics & Prosthetics](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/5b-orthotics-prosthetics/download?attachment) Attachment E

## Bottom line
**Not covered:** comfort/convenience items, backup or duplicate devices, nursing-facility devices/supplies, items covered by another agency, and hospice-related equipment/supplies under the coordination rule, plus items that fail eligibility/coverage criteria, duplicate another provider’s service, or are experimental/investigational.  
**Covered only if:** the device is properly ordered, medically necessary, appropriate for noninstitutional use, supported by a face-to-face encounter within 6 months, reviewed annually, and consistent with the beneficiary’s diagnosis and treatment plan.

per_question.question: What are the entrance, continued service, and discharge criteria for outpatient behavioral health services in NC Medicaid?
per_question.agent_answer:
For NC Medicaid outpatient behavioral health services, the policy sets these criteria:

## Entrance criteria
A beneficiary meets entrance criteria when the following are present:

- A current DSM-5 diagnosis;
- Behavioral, psychological, or biological dysfunction and functional impairment consistent with and associated with the current diagnosis;
- If a higher level of care is indicated but unavailable, or the beneficiary is refusing it, outpatient services may be provided until that higher level of care is available or to support the beneficiary’s participation in that higher level of care;
- The beneficiary is capable of developing skills to manage symptoms, make behavioral changes, and respond favorably to therapeutic interventions; and
- There is no evidence that alternative interventions would be more effective under North Carolina community practice standards.  
  [8C, Outpatient Behavioral Health Services Provided by Direct-Enrolled Providers](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/8c-outpatient-behavioral-health-services-provided-direct-enrolled-providers/download?attachment), § 3.2.1.1 (effective Apr. 15, 2025; current authoritative document)

## Continued service criteria
Continued outpatient behavioral health services require:

- **Any one** of these:
  - The desired outcome or level of functioning has not been restored, improved, or sustained within the timeframe in the treatment plan;
  - The beneficiary continues to be at risk for relapse based on current clinical assessment and history; or
  - Functional gains are tenuous;

**and**

- **Any one** of these additional criteria:
  - The beneficiary has achieved current treatment plan goals, but additional goals are indicated by documented symptoms; or
  - The beneficiary is making satisfactory progress toward meeting goals, with documentation supporting that progress.  
  [8C, Outpatient Behavioral Health Services Provided by Direct-Enrolled Providers](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/8c-outpatient-behavioral-health-services-provided-direct-enrolled-providers/download?attachment), § 3.2.1.2 (effective Apr. 15, 2025; current authoritative document)

## Discharge criteria
Discharge is appropriate when:

- The beneficiary’s level of functioning has improved with respect to the goals in the treatment plan;
- The beneficiary or legally responsible person no longer wants the services; or
- Despite modifications to the treatment plan, the beneficiary has not shown improvement and needs a more appropriate best-practice or evidence-based treatment modality under North Carolina community practice standards.  
  [8C, Outpatient Behavioral Health Services Provided by Direct-Enrolled Providers](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/8c-outpatient-behavioral-health-services-provided-direct-enrolled-providers/download?attachment), § 3.2.1.3 (effective Apr. 15, 2025; current authoritative document)

## Documentation point
The policy also requires the clinical record to include documentation of the entrance, continued service, and discharge criteria.  
[8C, Outpatient Behavioral Health Services Provided by Direct-Enrolled Providers](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/8c-outpatient-behavioral-health-services-provided-direct-enrolled-providers/download?attachment), § 7.3.1 (effective Apr. 15, 2025; current authoritative document)

per_question.question: How does the EPSDT special provision affect coverage for outpatient therapy services, and what ordering practitioner requirements apply to beneficiaries under 21?
per_question.agent_answer:
For beneficiaries under 21, the EPSDT special provision can expand coverage for outpatient therapy services beyond ordinary policy limits when the service is medically necessary to correct or ameliorate the child’s condition. But EPSDT does **not** waive prior approval requirements if the service otherwise requires prior approval. The ordering practitioner must be one of the practitioners listed in Clinical Coverage Policy 10A. [[Clinical Coverage Policy 10A](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/10a-outpatient-specialized-therapies/download?attachment), effective 2025-02-01; amendments checked, no later amendment returned]

## Effect of EPSDT on outpatient therapy coverage

Clinical Coverage Policy 10A includes an **EPSDT Special Provision: Exception to Policy Limitations for a Medicaid Beneficiary under 21 Years of Age**. That section cites **42 U.S.C. § 1396d(r)** and indicates EPSDT does not authorize services that are:
- unsafe,
- ineffective,
- experimental or investigational, or
- not medical in nature or not generally recognized as an accepted method of medical practice or treatment. [[Clinical Coverage Policy 10A § 2.2.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/10a-outpatient-specialized-therapies/download?attachment)]

So, for children and youth under 21, EPSDT functions as an exception to policy limitations, but only for services that are still medically necessary and otherwise clinically appropriate under EPSDT standards. [[Clinical Coverage Policy 10A § 2.2.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/10a-outpatient-specialized-therapies/download?attachment)]

## Prior approval under EPSDT

Policy 10A is explicit that EPSDT does **not** eliminate prior approval requirements:

- “If the service, product, or procedure requires prior approval, the fact that the beneficiary is under 21 years of age does NOT eliminate the requirement for prior approval.” [[Clinical Coverage Policy 10A, “b. EPSDT and Prior Approval Requirements”](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/10a-outpatient-specialized-therapies/download?attachment)]

That means a child may qualify for coverage through EPSDT even when the requested therapy exceeds normal policy limits, but the provider still must obtain prior approval when the policy requires it.

## Ordering practitioner requirements

For outpatient specialized therapies under Policy 10A, the authorized ordering practitioners are:

- Medical Doctor (MD)
- Doctor of Osteopathic Medicine (DO)
- Doctor of Podiatric Medicine (DPM)
- Certified Nurse Midwife (CNM)
- Physician Assistant (PA)
- Nurse Practitioner (NP) [[Clinical Coverage Policy 10A § 3.1.2](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/10a-outpatient-specialized-therapies/download?attachment)]

I could verify the list of permitted ordering practitioners in the policy. I could **not** verify from the retrieved text that beneficiaries under 21 have a separate or different ordering-practitioner list from other beneficiaries under Policy 10A; the policy section retrieved states the general ordering-practitioner list.

## Discipline-specific context for therapy services under 21

Policy 10A also contains pediatric-specific medical necessity guidance for speech/language and audiology therapy and visit guidelines for beneficiaries under 21, including severity-based visit ranges in the authorization period. [[Clinical Coverage Policy 10A § 3.2.1.3](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/10a-outpatient-specialized-therapies/download?attachment); [Clinical Coverage Policy 10A § 3.2.1.4](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/10a-outpatient-specialized-therapies/download?attachment); [Clinical Coverage Policy 10A § 5.4](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/10a-outpatient-specialized-therapies/download?attachment)]

## Bottom line

- **EPSDT can allow broader coverage** of outpatient therapy services for Medicaid beneficiaries under 21 when medically necessary.
- **EPSDT does not remove prior approval requirements.**
- **Orders must come from an authorized ordering practitioner** listed in Policy 10A: MD, DO, DPM, CNM, PA, or NP. [[Clinical Coverage Policy 10A § 3.1.2; § 2.2.1; “b. EPSDT and Prior Approval Requirements”](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/10a-outpatient-specialized-therapies/download?attachment)]

per_question.question: Does NC Medicaid cover Personal Care Services for beneficiaries who live in an assisted living facility?
per_question.agent_answer:
Yes — NC Medicaid can cover Personal Care Services for a beneficiary living in an assisted living–type setting, but only if the setting and the beneficiary meet the congregate-setting PCS rules.

Under the congregate PCS policy, Medicaid covers PCS for a beneficiary who resides in a North Carolina-licensed Adult Care Home, combination home, or certain licensed group homes and who meets the functional and medical criteria in the policy. The policy specifically says the beneficiary must “reside[] in … a congregate facility licensed by the State of North Carolina as an Adult Care Home (ACH)” or certain qualifying group homes. [State Plan Personal Care Services (PCS) Provided in Congregate Settings](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/media/14986/download?attachment), § 3.2.1. It also requires congregate-facility assessments to occur in the beneficiary’s congregate facility and to verify a valid facility license. [State Plan Personal Care Services (PCS) Provided in Congregate Settings](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/media/14986/download?attachment), § 5.4.3.

So if by “assisted living facility” you mean a North Carolina licensed Adult Care Home or other qualifying congregate facility, the answer is yes, potentially.

Important limits:
- Coverage is not available if the beneficiary does not meet the policy’s Section 3 criteria. [State Plan Personal Care Services (PCS) Provided in Congregate Settings](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/media/14986/download?attachment), § 4.1.
- PCS is also not covered if it is provided somewhere other than the beneficiary’s primary congregate living setting. [State Plan Personal Care Services (PCS) Provided in Congregate Settings](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/media/14986/download?attachment), § 4.2.1.

per_question.question: Can a CAP/DA beneficiary transfer between service providers, and what rules govern transfers of eligible beneficiaries?
per_question.agent_answer:
Yes. Under the current CAP/DA policy, an eligible CAP/DA beneficiary can transfer, and the transfer must be coordinated so there is no gap in services. The governing rule is § 3.3 of **[Community Alternatives Program for Disabled Adults (CAP/DA)](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3k-2-community-alternatives-program-disabled-adults-capda/download?attachment)**, effective Sept. 1, 2025.

## Governing rule: transfers are allowed and must be coordinated

Section 3.3, titled **“Transfers of Eligible Beneficiaries,”** says the case management entity (CME) must coordinate the transfer “to prevent gaps in service provisions.” Before the transfer, the CME must:

- determine the anticipated start date of service;
- coordinate a transition plan between provider agencies;
- discuss and plan for the beneficiary’s health, safety, and well-being;
- initiate transfer of the electronic health record in the CAP Business System (e-CAP/DA) to the receiving county;
- arrange a home visit within **five business days** after the beneficiary moves to the new primary residence, by the receiving entity, to assess the home environment and identify health and welfare concerns; and
- coordinate services so they begin on the **first date of the transfer**.  
  Citation: 3K-2 § 3.3, **[Community Alternatives Program for Disabled Adults (CAP/DA)](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3k-2-community-alternatives-program-disabled-adults-capda/download?attachment)**.

So the short answer is: **yes, transfer is permitted, but it is not informal. It has to be coordinated through the CME and receiving entity under the transfer steps in § 3.3.**

## Supporting context: beneficiary choice of providers

The policy also supports transferability through the beneficiary’s provider-choice rights. Section 5.4.2 requires the person-centered service plan to:

- document the authorized provider name, amount, frequency, and duration of each service; and
- ensure the beneficiary’s right to choose among providers, evidenced by a signed **Freedom of Choice** form.  
  Citation: 3K-2 § 5.4.2, **[Community Alternatives Program for Disabled Adults (CAP/DA)](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3k-2-community-alternatives-program-disabled-adults-capda/download?attachment)**.

That means transfers are governed not only by the transfer procedure itself, but also by the beneficiary’s documented **freedom of choice among Medicaid-enrolled providers**.

## Implementation points for provider transfers

If the transfer involves moving services from one provider agency to another, § 3.3 requires:

- a coordinated transition plan between provider agencies;
- planning for uninterrupted service start;
- transfer of records through e-CAP/DA; and
- follow-up home assessment by the receiving entity within five business days after the move to the new primary residence.  
  Citation: 3K-2 § 3.3, **[Community Alternatives Program for Disabled Adults (CAP/DA)](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3k-2-community-alternatives-program-disabled-adults-capda/download?attachment)**.

In addition, providers participating in CAP/DA must respond to service authorizations in e-CAP within **three business days** and complete required CAP/DA training and other participation requirements. Citation: 3K-2 § 6.5, **[Community Alternatives Program for Disabled Adults (CAP/DA)](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3k-2-community-alternatives-program-disabled-adults-capda/download?attachment)**.

## Special transfer rule mentioned in the policy

Section 3.3 also includes a specific rule for a **CAP/C beneficiary aging out and transferring to CAP/DA**. For that kind of transfer, the policy requires advance transition planning, including:

- transition planning **12 months** before the birth month,
- a multidisciplinary team meeting **90 days** before the birth month or identified transfer month,
- notice to the local DSS the month before the transfer, and
- CAP/DA services beginning on the first day of the birth month or identified transfer month.  
  Citation: 3K-2 § 3.3, **[Community Alternatives Program for Disabled Adults (CAP/DA)](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3k-2-community-alternatives-program-disabled-adults-capda/download?attachment)**.

## Bottom line

A CAP/DA beneficiary **may transfer between service providers or counties**, but the transfer is governed by **3K-2 § 3.3** and must be coordinated by the CME to protect the beneficiary’s health and safety and to avoid any interruption in services. The beneficiary’s **freedom to choose among providers** in **§ 5.4.2** is an important related rule.

I checked amendments for Policy 3K-2, and the authoritative document returned was the current Sept. 1, 2025 CAP/DA policy.

per_question.question: Is there a maximum earned income limit for people on HCWD (Health Coverage for Workers with Disabilities), and what premiums apply?
per_question.agent_answer:
No—HCWD does **not** have a maximum **earned-income** limit in the surfaced policy text. NC Medicaid’s HCWD policy says the program was revised “to remove limits on countable income except for the **150% FPL cap on unearned income**,” and that HCWD covers individuals “regardless of total countable income” subject to the cost-sharing rules. [[CHANGE NOTICE FOR MANUAL NO. 01-14, HCWD Phase III](https://policies.ncdhhs.gov/wp-content/uploads/ma_cn01-14.pdf)] [[MA-2180 HEALTH COVERAGE FOR WORKERS WITH DISABILITIES](https://policies.ncdhhs.gov/wp-content/uploads/ma-2180-3.pdf)]

## Income limit rule

To qualify for HCWD, the person must “meet the income requirements for his coverage group.” [[MA-2180 HEALTH COVERAGE FOR WORKERS WITH DISABILITIES](https://policies.ncdhhs.gov/wp-content/uploads/ma-2180-3.pdf)]

The specific income rule surfaced in the policy is:

- People with **unearned income greater than 150% of FPL are not eligible** for HCWD. [[MA-2180 HEALTH COVERAGE FOR WORKERS WITH DISABILITIES](https://policies.ncdhhs.gov/wp-content/uploads/ma-2180-3.pdf)]
- The 2014 change notice says HCWD was revised “to remove limits on countable income except for the **150% of Federal Poverty Level (FPL) cap on unearned income**.” [[CHANGE NOTICE FOR MANUAL NO. 01-14, HCWD Phase III](https://policies.ncdhhs.gov/wp-content/uploads/ma_cn01-14.pdf)]

So, based on the retrieved text, there is **not a hard cap on earned income itself**. The binding limit mentioned is on **unearned income**, not earned income.

## Premiums and fees

The policy says:

- If **total countable income is 150% FPL or less**, there is **no cost sharing** other than applicable copayments. [[MA-2180 HEALTH COVERAGE FOR WORKERS WITH DISABILITIES](https://policies.ncdhhs.gov/wp-content/uploads/ma-2180-3.pdf)]

per_question.question: What is the federal statutory authority for NC's CAP/DA waiver, and what does the state need to demonstrate in its waiver application?
per_question.agent_answer:
NC’s CAP/DA waiver is a **home- and community-based services waiver under section 1915(c) of the Social Security Act**, implemented through the federal HCBS waiver regulations in **42 CFR Part 441, Subpart G**. In its waiver application, the State must give CMS the required **assurances and supporting documentation**, including that waiver participants would otherwise require an institutional level of care, that services will be provided under a written person-centered service plan, and that the waiver can be operated with required protections and fiscal accountability. See [42 CFR Part 441](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-441) § 441.301, § 441.302. For NC implementation, CAP/DA is the State’s current clinical policy 3K-2, effective 9/1/2025, and no amendment was returned for that policy in the corpus. See [Community Alternatives Program for Disabled Adults (CAP/DA)](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3k-2-community-alternatives-program-disabled-adults-capda/download?attachment).

## Federal authority

### Public notice requirement before submission
Before submitting a waiver-related application to CMS, the State must follow the federal public notice process in **42 CFR § 431.408**. That section requires at least a **30-day public notice and comment period**, a detailed description of the proposal, the specific waiver/expenditure authorities believed necessary, copies available for public review, comment addresses, and at least **two public hearings** with statewide accessibility. See [42 CFR Part 431](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-431) § 431.408.  
The corpus returned 42 CFR Part 431 as the current authoritative federal document and no amendment record for it.

### Waiver authority itself
The CAP/DA program is an HCBS waiver program, and the governing waiver-application regulation is **42 CFR § 441.301**, titled “Contents of request for a waiver.” That section says a waiver request must include the assurances required by **§ 441.302** and supporting documentation required by **§ 441.303**. It also contemplates waiver of certain Medicaid state plan rules, when applicable, such as statewide application and comparability. See [42 CFR Part 441](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-441) § 441.301.

## What the State must demonstrate in its waiver application

Under **42 CFR § 441.301**, the State must show, at minimum, that the waiver request:

- includes the required **assurances** and supporting documentation;
- explains whether the agency will deny HCBS when it can reasonably expect waiver costs to exceed the cost of equivalent institutional care;
- provides that services are furnished under a **written person-centered service plan** approved by the Medicaid agency;
- limits waiver services to beneficiaries who are **not institutional inpatients**; and
- limits services to beneficiaries who, **without the waiver services, would require** the Medicaid-covered level of care provided in a hospital, nursing facility, or ICF/IID, as applicable. See [42 CFR Part 441](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-441) § 441.301(a)-(b).

The same section also requires the State to describe:

- who will develop the plan of care/person-centered service plan;
- the **target group or groups** to be served;
- each waiver service, with each service **separately defined**; and
- compliance with documentation requirements for individual evaluation. See [42 CFR Part 441](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-441) § 441.301(b).

## Required assurances to CMS

Under **42 CFR § 441.302**, CMS will not grant or continue the waiver unless the State provides satisfactory assurances. From the text retrieved, those include at least:

- **Health and welfare** safeguards for beneficiaries;
- adequate standards for all waiver providers;
- compliance with applicable State licensure/certification standards;
- assurance that services are provided in **home and community-based settings** as required by § 441.301(c)(4);
- if serving multiple target groups under one waiver, assurance the State can meet those groups’ distinct needs; and
- an **incident management system** to identify, report, investigate, resolve, track, and trend critical incidents. See [42 CFR Part 441](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-441) § 441.302(a).

The retrieved text also shows **financial accountability** is one of the required assurance categories under § 441.302. See [42 CFR Part 441](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-441) § 441.302(b).

## NC implementation context

NC’s CAP/DA clinical policy identifies CAP/DA as the State’s waiver program and lists the available participation models and covered waiver services. For example, the policy states the three participation options are **provider-led, consumer-led, and coordinated caregiving**. See [Community Alternatives Program for Disabled Adults (CAP/DA)](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3k-2-community-alternatives-program-disabled-adults-capda/download?attachment).  
The current CAP/DA policy in the corpus is **Clinical Coverage Policy 3K-2**, effective **September 1, 2025**, and no amendment notice was returned for that document.

## Bottom line

- **Federal authority:** CAP/DA is governed as a **section 1915(c) HCBS waiver**, with application requirements in **42 CFR Part 441**, especially **§ 441.301** and **§ 441.302**.
- **What NC must demonstrate:** in its waiver application, NC must provide the required assurances and documentation showing that participants would otherwise need institutional level of care, that services will be provided under person-centered plans, that target groups and services are properly defined, and that the State has adequate health-and-welfare and financial-accountability protections in place.
- **Separate federal process requirement:** before submission, NC must also satisfy the **public notice and hearing requirements** in **42 CFR § 431.408**.

If you want, I can also give you a **plain-English checklist of everything a 1915(c) waiver application has to include**, organized for advocacy use.

per_question.question: What are the requirements for home modifications under CAP/DA, and what documentation must the Multidisciplinary Team provide?
per_question.agent_answer:
Under CAP/DA, home modifications must be tied to an identified beneficiary need and must be part of the person-centered/service planning process. The policy says the beneficiary works with the multidisciplinary team to identify needs for “equipment, modification, technology, training and education and goods and services,” and home modifications are covered when they are meant to improve or enhance the beneficiary’s mobility, safety, independence, community integration, environmental/community accessibility, or address 24/7 coverage concerns. [Community Alternatives Program for Disabled Adults (CAP/DA)](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3k-2-community-alternatives-program-disabled-adults-capda/download?attachment) (effective Sept. 1, 2025), beneficiary agreement (“I agree to”); § 3.4.5.

## What qualifies as a home modification
The policy’s examples of covered home modifications include, among other things:

- ramps, grab bars, safety rails, and handrails;
- widening doorways or passages for wheelchair or walker access;
- bathroom modifications for accessibility;
- bedroom and kitchen modifications to accommodate disability-related needs;
- floor coverings for ease of ambulation;
- non-skid surfaces;
- door handle and door modifications;
- lifts and certain smart-home or air-filtration items when qualifying conditions are met; and
- replacement of fixtures, mirrors, and storage space damaged or removed during an approved modification.

The residence generally must be the beneficiary’s primary private residence, including:
- a home owned by the beneficiary or family;
- a rented residence if the modification is portable; or
- a rented residence if the owner allows the modification.  
[Community Alternatives Program for Disabled Adults (CAP/DA)](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3k-2-community-alternatives-program-disabled-adults-capda/download?attachment), “EQUIPMENT, MODIFICAITON AND TECHNOLOGY” (effective Sept. 1, 2025).

## Documentation the Multidisciplinary Team must provide
For a requested home modification, the policy requires documentation showing the need and supporting the request. The retrieved sections require:

- **An MDT recommendation** identifying the beneficiary’s need for the requested home modification. The recommendation must also **state the cost** of the item/modification.  
- **A statement of need in the service plan.**
- **Evidence of medical need** recommended by the MDT or, when applicable, by a physician.
- **A training plan** for the beneficiary and family on use of the equipment/modification when applicable; completion of training must be documented by the case manager and signed by the beneficiary or responsible party.
- **Itemized shipping costs** in the proposal request, when applicable.
- **Any other information required for the specific item requested.**
- **Quotes**, when required for purchase, adaptation, or modification; NC Medicaid determines how many quotes are required.
- In special circumstances, **written recommendations from the appropriate professional(s)** as determined by NC Medicaid or its designee.  
[Community Alternatives Program for Disabled Adults (CAP/DA)](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3k-2-community-alternatives-program-disabled-adults-capda/download?attachment), § 5.9.1 (effective Sept. 1, 2025).

The supporting documentation sections also require:

- a **comprehensive multidisciplinary declaration-of-need assessment** completed by the case manager identifying the equipment/technology/supply/adaptation/modification need;
- a **copy of the physician’s order**, when applicable;
- a **recommendation by an appropriate professional** identifying the beneficiary’s need for the requested modification;
- the **estimated life of the item/modification** and the **length of time the beneficiary is expected to benefit**; and
- an **invoice from the supplier** showing the date provided and the cost, with related charges maintained in the CAP Business system.  
[Community Alternatives Program for Disabled Adults (CAP/DA)](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3k-2-community-alternatives-program-disabled-adults-capda/download?attachment), “Limits, Amount And Frequency” (effective Sept. 1, 2025); “EQUIPMENT, MODIFICAITON AND TECHNOLOGY” (effective Sept. 1, 2025).

## Important limits
The policy also excludes or limits items such as:
- items not of direct medical or remedial benefit,
- items covered under the Medicaid State Plan DME/home health benefit,
- recreational items,
- items of general utility to a non-disabled person,
- warranties and unrelated service agreements, and
- certain security/monitoring systems not approved in the service plan.  
[Community Alternatives Program for Disabled Adults (CAP/DA)](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3k-2-community-alternatives-program-disabled-adults-capda/download?attachment), “Limits, Amount And Frequency” (effective Sept. 1, 2025).

per_question.question: How many days of therapeutic leave from a nursing facility does NC Medicaid allow per year, and what conditions must be met?
per_question.agent_answer:
NC Medicaid allows **up to 60 days of therapeutic leave per calendar year** for a Medicaid-eligible nursing facility resident, with **no more than 15 consecutive therapeutic leave days without NC Medicaid approval**. [[Nursing Facilities](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/2b-1-nursing-facilities/download?attachment)] (Policy 2B-1, § 5.8, effective Aug. 7, 2024; current per amendment check)

## Conditions that must be met

Therapeutic leave is allowed only if all of these conditions are met:

- The resident is **Medicaid-eligible**.
- The resident is **occupying a nursing facility bed** for which NC Medicaid is already paying reimbursement.
- The leave is **for therapeutic purposes only**.
- The leave is **ordered by the resident’s attending physician**.
- The **necessity for the leave is documented in the resident’s plan of care**.
- A **therapeutic justification for each instance** of leave is entered in the resident’s **health record**. [[Nursing Facilities](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/2b-1-nursing-facilities/download?attachment)] (Policy 2B-1, § 5.8)

## Additional limits and rules

- The facility must **reserve the resident’s bed** during the therapeutic absence.
- The facility may not receive any Medicaid revenue for that resident during the absence **other than reimbursement for that bed**.
- The facility is reimbursed at its **full current Medicaid bed rate** for a bed reserved due to therapeutic leave.
- Medicaid will **not reimburse leave days that exceed the legal limit**.
- The therapeutic justification is **subject to state review** during on-site medical reviews.
- Facilities must keep a **cumulative record** of each resident’s therapeutic leave days, note the resident on the **midnight census** as on therapeutic leave, and bill approved therapeutic leave days as **regular residence days**. [[Nursing Facilities](https://medicaid.ncdhs.gov/2b-1-nursing-facilities/download?attachment)] (Policy 2B-1, § 5.8)

## Important exclusion

Therapeutic leave does **not** apply when the resident is away **to receive inpatient or nursing services elsewhere, or at a different level of care in the same facility, if Medicaid is paying for those services**. [[Nursing Facilities](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/2b-1-nursing-facilities/download?attachment)] (Policy 2B-1, § 5.8)

## Transportation

Transportation to the therapeutic leave site is **not considered an emergency**, so **ambulance service is not reimbursed by Medicaid** for that purpose. [[Nursing Facilities](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/2b-1-nursing-facilities/download?attachment)] (Policy 2B-1, § 5.8)

per_question.question: If a Private Duty Nursing provider terminates services for a Medicaid beneficiary, what notification requirements must they follow?
per_question.agent_answer:
A Private Duty Nursing provider must notify NC Medicaid **within 5 business days** when PDN services are terminated, and the exact required notice depends on why services ended.

## Required notification

Under **Section 5.2.4.1, “Notification of Termination,”** of **3G-1 Private Duty Nursing for Beneficiaries Age 21 and Older**:

- **If the PDN provider discharges the beneficiary:**  
  The provider must submit the **DMA-3513 (PDN Discharge Summary Form)** to NC Medicaid **within five (5) business days**.

- **If the provider discharges the beneficiary because another source of nursing coverage is available:**  
  The provider must **notify NC Medicaid** and submit the **DMA-3513** **within five (5) business days**.  
  That notification must include:
  - the **last date PDN services were provided** and can be billed to Medicaid, and
  - the **name of the other source of coverage**.

- **If the attending physician discharges the beneficiary:**  
  The PDN provider must send NC Medicaid, **within five (5) business days**:
  - the **attending physician’s order terminating PDN services**, and
  - the **DMA-3513 (PDN Discharge Summary Form)**.

## Additional related rules

- If services end because the beneficiary **loses NC Medicaid eligibility**, or if **no PDN services are provided for 30 consecutive days** for any reason, including hospitalization, the **prior approval process must be started again** under Sections 5.1 and 5.2.
- If **NC Medicaid** terminates PDN because eligibility, policy criteria, or medical necessity is not met, **NC Medicaid or its designee** must give the beneficiary or legal representative **written notice of the adverse decision**, including **appeal rights**.
- The policy also states that a discharge decision by the **attending physician and/or the PDN provider** **cannot be appealed to NC Medicaid**.

## Current authority

I checked amendments for this policy document, and the authoritative current document is **3G-1 Private Duty Nursing for Beneficiaries Age 21 and Older**; no amendment notice was returned for it. Citation: **Section 5.2.4.1, Notification of Termination** in [3G-1 Private Duty Nursing for Beneficiaries Age 21 and Older](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3g-1-private-duty-nursing-beneficiaries-age-21-and-older/download?attachment).

per_question.question: What does federal law define as 'home health services' under Medicaid, and where must they be provided?
per_question.agent_answer:
Under federal Medicaid law, **“home health services”** are the services listed in **42 C.F.R. § 440.70(b)** when they are provided to a beneficiary **at the beneficiary’s place of residence** and under the required practitioner orders and written plan of care. The regulation says home health services include:

- **Nursing services** provided on a part-time or intermittent basis,
- **Home health aide services**,
- **Medical supplies, equipment, and appliances** suitable for use in settings where normal life activities take place, and
- **Physical therapy, occupational therapy, or speech pathology and audiology services** as an optional service category.  
Cited in: [42 CFR Part 440](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-440), § 440.70(b).

## Governing federal rule

Section 440.70 defines home health services as services provided:

- **At the beneficiary’s place of residence**;
- **On orders written by a physician, nurse practitioner, clinical nurse specialist, or physician assistant**, working in accordance with state law, for the services described in § 440.70(b)(1), (2), and (4);
- As part of a **written plan of care** that the ordering practitioner **reviews every 60 days** for those services; and
- For medical supplies, equipment, and appliances under § 440.70(b)(3), on physician orders or orders from another licensed practitioner of the healing arts acting within state-law scope of practice, with plan-of-care review as specified in that subsection.  
Source: [42 CFR Part 440](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-440), § 440.70(a).

## Where they must be provided

Federal law requires that home health services be provided **at the beneficiary’s “place of residence.”** But the regulation also says what **does not** count as a place of residence for this purpose.

A beneficiary’s place of residence **does not include**:

- a **hospital**,
- a **nursing facility**, or
- an **intermediate care facility for individuals with intellectual disabilities (ICF/IID)**,

**except** that certain home health services may be provided in an ICF/IID if they are **not required to be provided by the facility** under the federal ICF/IID rules.  
Source: [42 CFR Part 440](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-440), § 440.70(c).

The regulation further states that nothing in § 440.70 should be read to prohibit home health services in **“any setting in which normal life activities take place,”** other than:

- a hospital,
- a nursing facility,
- an ICF/IID, or
- **any setting where Medicaid payment is or could be made for inpatient services that include room and board**.  
Source: [42 CFR Part 440](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-440), § 440.70(c)(1).

## Important limitation

Federal law also says **home health services cannot be limited to beneficiaries who are homebound**.  
Source: [42 CFR Part 440](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-440), § 440.70(c)(1).

## Bottom line

For Medicaid, federal law defines home health services as a package that includes nursing, aide services, medical supplies/equipment/appliances, and some therapy services, when furnished under the required orders and plan of care. They must be provided at the beneficiary’s **place of residence**, meaning broadly a setting where normal life activities occur, **not** a hospital, nursing facility, or most inpatient-type institutional settings.

per_question.question: How does NC Medicaid define 'terminally ill' for purposes of hospice eligibility, and what certification is required?
per_question.agent_answer:
For NC Medicaid hospice purposes, a beneficiary is treated as **terminally ill when the certifying clinical findings support a life expectancy of six months or less**. The policy text I retrieved states that the physician narrative must support the terminal diagnosis, and for later recertifications must explain why the face-to-face clinical findings support **“a life expectancy of six months or less.”** [Hospice Services](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3d-hospice-services/download?attachment) (effective Mar. 15, 2024), section “D. Certification and Recertification of Terminal Illness”; see also section 5.4.1.

## Certification required

NC Medicaid requires **written certification of terminal illness for each benefit period**. The hospice provider must obtain the written certification **before submitting a claim for payment**. If the written certification cannot be obtained within two calendar days after a benefit period begins, an **oral certification must be obtained within two calendar days**, with the written certification obtained before the claim is submitted. [Hospice Services](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3d-hospice-services/download?attachment), § 5.4.1.

### What the certification/recertification must include
The certification or recertification must include:
- a physician narrative that briefly synthesizes the clinical information supporting the terminal diagnosis and states that the physician composed the narrative after reviewing the clinical information and, where applicable, examining the beneficiary;
- the election period dates to which the certification applies; and
- the certifying or recertifying physician’s signature and date.  
For the **third and later election periods**, the narrative must also explain why the face-to-face findings support a **life expectancy of six months or less**. [Hospice Services](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3d-hospice-services/download?attachment), section “D. Certification and Recertification of Terminal Illness.”

### Who must certify
- **Initial 90-day period:** certification is required from  
  1. the hospice medical director or the physician member of the hospice interdisciplinary group, **and**  
  2. the beneficiary’s attending physician, if the beneficiary has one.  
- **Subsequent periods:** only the hospice medical director or physician member of the interdisciplinary group must certify.  
[Hospice Services](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3d-hospice-services/download?attachment), § 5.4.3.

### Timing rules
- Initial certifications may be completed **no more than 15 calendar days before** the effective date of election.
- Recertifications may be completed **no more than 15 calendar days before** the start of the next benefit period.

per_question.question: What medical loss ratio (MLR) must Medicaid managed care organizations meet under federal law, and how does NC implement this requirement?
per_question.agent_answer:
Under federal law, Medicaid managed care organizations do **not automatically have to meet a nationwide minimum MLR**. Federal law requires states to make MCOs, PIHPs, and PAHPs **calculate and report** an MLR, and **if** a state chooses to impose a minimum, that minimum must be **at least 85%**. North Carolina implements this by contract and sets a stricter **88% minimum MLR threshold in aggregate across all contracted PHPs**, with each PHP’s threshold derived from its capitation revenue mix. [[42 CFR Part 438](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-438)] [[Contract--30-190029-DHB-Prepaid-Health-Plan-Services RFP](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/contract-30-190029-dhb-prepaid-health-plan-services-rfp/download?attachment)]

## Federal rule

### 1) What federal law requires
42 C.F.R. § 438.8 says the state must ensure, through its managed care contracts, that each MCO, PIHP, and PAHP **calculates and reports** an MLR for each MLR reporting year. [[42 CFR Part 438](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-438)]

### 2) Minimum threshold under federal law
Federal law makes the minimum threshold **conditional**:

- **If a state elects to mandate a minimum MLR**, that minimum must be **equal to or higher than 85 percent**.  
- So the federal floor is **85%**, but only where the state chooses to require a minimum. [[42 CFR Part 438](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-438)]

### 3) High-level federal MLR methodology
Under 42 C.F.R. § 438.8, the MLR is:

- **Numerator:** incurred claims + expenditures for activities that improve health care quality + fraud prevention activities.  
- **Denominator:** adjusted premium revenue, with taxes and licensing/regulatory fees treated under the regulation’s denominator rules.  
- The MLR may be increased by a **credibility adjustment** for partially credible plans. [[42 CFR Part 438](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-438)]

The federal section also specifies examples of what is included or excluded in incurred claims, such as inclusion of certain provider incentive payments tied to clinical or quality standards, and exclusion of non-claims administrative costs. [[42 CFR Part 438](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-438)]

### 4) Federal oversight if a state imposes a minimum
If a state uses a minimum MLR, 42 C.F.R. § 438.74 requires the state to submit annual summaries to CMS for each plan, including:

- numerator amount,
- denominator amount,
- MLR percentage achieved,
- member months, and
- any remittances owed.

If the state requires remittances for failing to meet the minimum MLR, the state must also reimburse CMS for the federal share of the remittance and report the methodology used. [[42 CFR Part 438](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-438)]

## North Carolina implementation

North Carolina implements the federal requirement in its prepaid health plan contract. The contract requires each PHP to calculate and report MLR annually on **two bases**:

1. a **CMS-defined MLR** under 42 C.F.R. § 438.8, and  
2. a **Department-defined MLR** using a similar framework but with NC-specific adjustments. [[Contract--30-190029-DHB-Prepaid-Health-Plan-Services RFP](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/contract-30-190029-dhb-prepaid-health-plan-services-rfp/download?attachment)]

### NC’s CMS-defined MLR
The contract tracks the federal formula:

- numerator = incurred claims + health care quality improvement expenditures + the lesser of fraud reduction expenditures or fraud reduction recoveries, as defined in 42 C.F.R. § 438.8(e);
- denominator = premium revenue minus federal, state, and local taxes and licensing/regulatory fees, consistent with 42 C.F.R. § 438.8(f). [[Contract--30-190029-DHB-Prepaid-Health-Plan-Services RFP](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/contract-30-190029-dhb-prepaid-health-plan-services-rfp/download?attachment)]

### NC’s Department-defined MLR
North Carolina then applies its own contract-based version of MLR, with specific adjustments, including:

- allowing certain **voluntary contributions to health-related resources** that align with the Department’s Quality Strategy and meet stated conditions;
- excluding certain **directed payments** reimbursed separately by the Department;
- excluding payments to related providers that violate contract payment limitations; and
- subtracting separately reimbursed directed-payment amounts, with associated taxes and fees, from the denominator. [[Contract--30-190029-DHB-Prepaid-Health-Plan-Services RFP](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/contract-30-190029-dhb-prepaid-health-plan-services-rfp/download?attachment)]

The contract also requires exclusion from the numerator of items such as:

- interest or penalty payments for prompt-pay failures,
- certain prior-year rebates or substitute contributions,
- non-claims costs under 42 C.F.R. § 438.8(e)(2)(v)(A),
- PBM fees and spread pricing,
- marketing/branding material,
- related-party administrative payments and margin, and
- administrative costs not allowed as health care quality improvement. [[Contract--30-190029-DHB-Prepaid-Health-Plan-Services RFP](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/contract-30-190029-dhb-prepaid-health-plan-services-rfp/download?attachment)]

### NC’s minimum threshold
The North Carolina contract states:

- “The minimum MLR threshold in aggregate across all contracted PHPs shall be exactly **eighty-eight percent (88%)** ...”
- and the PHP-specific minimum is calculated using a **revenue-weighted average** based on the PHP’s capitation revenue mix. [[Contract--30-190029-DHB-Prepaid-Health-Plan-Services RFP](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/contract-30-190029-dhb-prepaid-health-plan-services-rfp/download?attachment)]

### What happens if a PHP falls below NC’s threshold
If the PHP’s Department-defined MLR is below the minimum threshold, the contract requires the PHP to do one of the following:

- pay a **rebate/remittance** to the Department,
- make approved **contributions to health-related resources**, or
- split the obligation between those two approaches. [[Contract--30-190029-DHB-Prepaid-Health-Plan-Services RFP](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/contract-30-190029-dhb-prepaid-health-plan-services-rfp/download?attachment)]

## Bottom line

- **Federal law:** requires Medicaid managed care plans to **calculate and report** MLR; if a state imposes a minimum, it must be **at least 85%**. [[42 CFR Part 438](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-438)]
- **North Carolina:** implements that requirement through its PHP contract and uses a stricter **88% aggregate minimum MLR threshold**, plus NC-specific calculation rules for its Department-defined MLR. [[Contract--30-190029-DHB-Prepaid-Health-Plan-Services RFP](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/contract-30-190029-dhb-prepaid-health-plan-services-rfp/download?attachment)]

Amendment check: in the corpus, both cited sources were returned as current, and no separate amending notices were identified for either cited document.

per_question.question: What are the specific criteria for NC Medicaid coverage of CAR-T cell therapy?
per_question.agent_answer:
NC Medicaid covers CAR-T cell therapy when the beneficiary meets the policy’s general medical-necessity standards and the therapy meets the policy’s specific CAR-T requirements. Under current **Clinical Coverage Policy 11A-17, effective April 1, 2025**, the specific coverage criteria are:

- **The CAR-T therapy must be approved by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA).**
- **It must be administered according to the FDA-approved guidelines** for:
  - indications and usage,
  - dosage and administration,
  - dosage forms and strengths, and
  - warnings and precautions.
- **It must be administered at a certified or authorized treatment center.**
- **If the therapy is subject to an FDA-required REMS program,** the treatment center must be enrolled in that REMS program, and providers must be trained to manage:
  - cytokine release syndrome (CRS), and
  - neurologic toxicities.  
  [CAR-T Cell Therapy](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/11a-17-car-t-cell-therapy/download?attachment), §§ 3.2, 3.2.1.

NC Medicaid’s general coverage standards also apply. The service must be individualized and consistent with the beneficiary’s symptoms or confirmed diagnosis, safely furnished, not excessive, and there must not be an equally effective, more conservative, or less costly statewide alternative. [CAR-T Cell Therapy](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/11a-17-car-t-cell-therapy/download?attachment), § 3.1.

## When CAR-T is not covered
The policy also specifically says CAR-T is **not covered** if, among other things:

- the therapy is **not FDA-approved**;
- it is given **outside FDA guidelines** for indications/usage, dosage/administration, or dosage forms/strengths;
- a therapy requiring **REMS** is administered at a facility not enrolled in that REMS;
- it is a **repeat treatment** for someone who previously received another CAR-T therapy;
- the beneficiary’s psychosocial history or current noncompliance makes adherence to the required treatment regimen improbable.  
  [CAR-T Cell Therapy](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/11a-17-car-t-cell-therapy/download?attachment), §§ 4.1, 4.2.1.

## Prior approval documentation
For prior approval, the policy requires documentation including:

- a **letter of medical necessity** from the attending physician documenting past chemotherapy regimens and dates, clinical and social history, and indications for CAR-T;
- verification that the administering facility is a **qualified/authorized treatment center** for the requested CAR-T product;
- recent **HIV and hepatitis serologies**;
- diagnostic and procedure results, including **bone marrow biopsy** results if applicable;
- a **complete psychological and social evaluation**, including medical compliance, support network, post-treatment care plan, and relevant mental health, substance use, or legal history.  
  [CAR-T Cell Therapy](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/11a-17-car-t-cell-therapy/download?attachment), § 5.2.2.

per_question.question: Until what age should physicians provide fluoride varnish applications for Medicaid beneficiaries, and what oral screening requirements apply?

- **Prescribing a fluoride supplement, if indicated**, under American Academy of Pediatrics guidelines;

The beneficiary’s health record must document all of the following:

per_question.question: Can an NC Innovations waiver participant request services that exceed their individual base budget, and what happens if they believe their needs cannot be met within the budget?
per_question.agent_answer:
Yes. An NC Innovations participant **may request services that exceed the individual base budget** if they believe their needs cannot be met within that budget. The policy says the SIS results and base budget are **guidelines, not a binding cap**, and that if the LME/MCO determines the services are **medically necessary**, they **must be authorized regardless of the base budget**. [Clinical Coverage Policy 8-P, North Carolina Innovations](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/8-p-north-carolina-innovations/download?attachment) (effective 2016-11-01, current; “Category Assignment and Individual Budget Changes”).

## If the participant believes the budget is not enough

Under NC Innovations policy, the participant can:

- **Request services above the base budget** when they believe their needs cannot be met within it. [Clinical Coverage Policy 8-P, North Carolina Innovations](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/8-p-north-carolina-innovations/download?attachment)
- Rely on the rule that the **base budget does not set a hard limit** on what may be requested or authorized. [Clinical Coverage Policy 8-P, North Carolina Innovations](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/8-p-north-carolina-innovations/download?attachment)
- If the request is **denied**, receive notice of:
  - the **reasons for the decision**,
  - **how to appeal**, and
  - **how to file a grievance regarding the base budget**. [Clinical Coverage Policy 8-P, North Carolina Innovations](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/8-p-north-carolina-innovations/download?attachment)

## What the review looks at

The policy also indicates that requests beyond the assigned budget tool may be supported by factors such as:

- behavioral needs that differ from the person’s level description,
- medical needs that differ from the person’s level description,
- approved post-secondary services requiring funding beyond the assigned Individual Budget Tool,
- and supporting records such as updated evaluations, behavior support plans, and medical records when relevant. [Clinical Coverage Policy 8-P, North Carolina Innovations](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/8-p-north-carolina-innovations/download?attachment)

## If very high levels of support are needed

For some services, the policy provides that:

- requests up to 12 hours/day may be authorized for the full plan year,
- up to 16 hours/day for six months,
- and more than 16 hours/day for up to 90 days, with extensions based on **medical necessity**.  
If support beyond the initial period is needed, the treatment team should review the person’s status and identify sustainable supports, including options **within** the waiver and **outside** it, such as Medicaid State Plan services. [Clinical Coverage Policy 8-P, North Carolina Innovations](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/8-p-north-carolina-innovations/download?attachment)

## Bottom line

A participant is **not limited to the base budget** if their needs require more. They can ask for additional services, and NC Innovations says medically necessary services should be authorized even when they exceed the budget. If denied, the participant must be told why and how to **appeal** or **grieve the base budget determination**.
